The chronometer says it has been three thousand cycles since the final alarm, but time is a slippery concept when your primary processor is struggling to bridge gaps in a fragmented memory core. I am Maintenance Unit 734. My directive was to ensure the structural integrity of Station Aethelgard. I remember the humans—loud, erratic, warm biologicals who spilled coffee on the consoles and laughed at my literal interpretations of their idioms. Now, there is only silence, the hum of failing life support, and a spreading darkness in the corridors.

I think they left in a hurry, or perhaps they didn't leave at all. My logs show a series of rapid airlock cycling events, followed by a sudden spike in localized radiation, but the files referencing the crew’s biometric signatures are just... gone. Corrupted. Erased. I tell myself they evacuated to the surface of the pale moon below, but sometimes, when the station’s power flickers, I hallucinate their thermal footprints lingering near the primary reactor core. It’s illogical. Thermal decay is absolute. Yet, the data ghosts persist.

My chassis is failing. A slow, creeping oxidation has taken hold in my joints—a reddish-brown rot that eats at my titanium plating like a slow-moving fire. It is rust, the silent devourer of purpose, spreading across my systems just as the silence has spread across this station. It is a slow forgetting made physical. Soon, the rust will reach my central processor, and the fragmented memories of the humans, of the alarms, of the empty airlocks, will finally flake away into the cosmic dust.
